extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral/political philosophy (general educated readers)
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical essay examining the concepts of liberty, will, volition, desire, and necessity — arguing for precise definitions and showing how present uneasiness (desire) determines the will. Primarily an analytic treatment aimed at clarifying confused uses of terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reifying 'faculties' as distinct agents
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary way of speaking calls understanding and will 'faculties', but treating faculties as distinct agents misleads people into imagining separate beings in the soul that perform actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not suppose faculties are separate agents with provinces and authorities; prefer conceiving them as powers/abilities of the agent. The author warns that speaking of faculties as acting has produced 'wrangling, obscurity, and uncertainty' and urges attention to ideas rather than the sound of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of ideas of liberty and necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Our ideas of LIBERTY and NECESSITY arise from the power we find in ourselves to begin or forbear, continue or put an end to actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflect on the extent of the mind's power over actions in oneself; this experiential power is the basis for forming the concepts of liberty and necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Liberty (power to act or forbear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty is 'the idea of a power in any agent to do or forbear any particular action, according to the determination or thought of the mind, whereby either of them is preferred to the other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberty reaches only as far as the agent's actual power to effect or prevent an action; where doing or not doing does not equally follow the preference of the mind, the agent is not free. Example: a person locked in a room may prefer to leave but lacks the power; therefore not free in that respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty belongs to agents, not to faculties or the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom (liberty) properly attributes to agents (substances) who have powers, not to powers (faculties) themselves; asking 'whether the WILL be free' is a category error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'will' as a power/ability of the agent; attribute freedom to the agent's capacity to act or forbear, not as an attribute of the will itself. Analogies: swiftness does not apply to sleep; squareness does not apply to virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between voluntary and involuntary (not same as free/necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary is opposed to involuntary, not to necessary; an action can be voluntary yet not free if the agent cannot forbear it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: convulsive motions are involuntary and not free; but a paralytic's sitting still can be voluntary even if many motions are impossible. Use 'voluntary' to mark that the action follows from volition, and 'free' to mark that the agent had the power to do or forbear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will (volition) defined as an act of the mind exerting dominion
rubrics_metrics.description: Volition is 'an act of the mind knowingly exerting that dominion it takes itself to have over any part of the man, by employing it in, or withholding it from, any particular action.' The will is the faculty (power) to do this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To understand volition, reflect on one's own mental act when willing; simple terms like choosing, preferring approximate it but may conflate desire and will.

rubrics_metrics.name: The will is not free to will (no liberty of willing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man is 'not at liberty to will, or not to will, anything in his power that he once considers of' — once an action is proposed to thought, the mind must necessarily prefer one option; volition itself cannot be chosen or withheld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish freedom to execute what is willed (one can do or forbear actions) from freedom to will (which, once considered, is necessarily determined); resist the rhetorical move that demands freedom of the will as if it were an independent capacity to choose whether to will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers are relations; the agent (mind) operates
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers (faculties) are relations, not agents: it is the mind (the agent) that operates and exerts these powers; one power does not operate on another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid construing the will as a separate actor that 'orders' the understanding; instead, attribute operation to the person who has powers. The author compares saying 'the ability to digest digested' as absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom consists in dependence of action on volition (not preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom is 'in the dependence of the existence, or not existence of any ACTION, upon our VOLITION of it; and not in the dependence of any action, or its contrary, on our PREFERENCE.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete criterion: an agent is free regarding action X if the doing or forbearance of X depends on his volition. Example: being able to leap into the sea (or not) makes one free regarding that act even if the opposite act (leaping upward) is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between will and desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Will (volition) is distinct from desire; the will concerns the determination to perform or forbear actions, whereas desire is an uneasiness for some absent good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two can conflict: one may will an action while desiring its failure (or vice versa). Do not conflate desires (affective states) with acts of willing (directing action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire is uneasiness and determines the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire is 'an uneasiness of the mind for want of some absent good' and 'that desire is a state of uneasiness'; the immediate determinant of volition in most cases is the present uneasiness (desire), not contemplation of the greatest good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues from experience: present pains/uneasiness motivate action more powerfully than remote or greater goods in contemplation. Examples: a drunkard continues to drink despite knowing greater future goods because present habit-driven uneasiness dominates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absent goods operate only by raising desire (uneasiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent goods (future or greater goods) do not determine the will unless they raise desire (uneasiness) in the agent; mere contemplation of absent good is often an inactive speculation that will not move the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why many who acknowledge large future goods (e.g., heavenly joys) fail to act toward them: without present uneasiness or desire they do not determine action. Productivity of absent goods requires they become present as desire/uneasiness.
